pending_articles.title: From hands to tools: evidence for evolutionary precursors of tool processing in macaque cortex.
pending_articles.content: In humans, hands are animate effectors and tools are visually dissimilar inanimate objects, yet the brain represents them in closely related cortical systems. Whether this coupling depends uniquely on human tool knowledge or reflects a conserved property of primate cortex is unknown. Using whole brain fMRI (0.22 cubic mm voxels) in macaques viewing images of hands, tools, and other objects, we found that inferotemporal cortex largely followed the animate/inanimate division, with only a few small hand-tool preferring sites. In contrast, parietal and prefrontal areas showed hand-tool representational similarities that were best matched by a neural-network model trained on fine-grained human hand-object interactions rather than by networks optimized for static object recognition or general action recognition. Volumetric functional ultrasound imaging (0.0023 cubic mm voxels) independently showed that tool responses were spatially aligned with human hand, but not monkey hand, responses in posterior parietal cortex. Macaque cortex thus represents tools in relation to the hand even without habitual tool use, consistent with an evolutionarily conserved action related scaffold that may be shaped by longterm visual exposure to human hand tool interactions.

pending_articles.title: Determinants of domain-specific cognitive impairment after stroke: a mega-analysis of 13 acute ischaemic stroke cohorts
pending_articles.content: The relationship between brain lesions and cognition is enigmatic. Apparently similar lesions can produce different outcomes. Stroke provides a prototypical model to understand how lesion anatomy, network disruption, prior injury and patient characteristics shape impairment. We analysed 3,034 patients from 13 acute ischaemic stroke cohorts, integrating infarct size and location, structural and functional lesion network mapping, pre-existing cerebrovascular injury, and demographic and clinical characteristics to predict impairment across six cognitive domains within one year after stroke. Infarct topography and connectivity improved prediction for six of seven outcomes over demographic, clinical and infarct-size information alone. Structural lesion connectivity accounted for most gains, with additional gains from topography and connectivity of pre-existing vascular lesions. Across domains, gains rested on left anterior thalamic connectivity plus domain-specific anatomy. Our findings establish, at unprecedented scale, that understanding lesion-cognition relationships requires looking beyond the lesion to networks, prior brain pathology and individual context.

pending_articles.title: Spectral power-laws emerge naturally from realistic tuning curve heterogeneity
pending_articles.content: How the brain represents the outside world with precision and allows for generalization is a fundamental question in neuroscience. One way of interpreting activity in neural systems is by contrasting two opposing coding principles: efficient coding, which produces high-dimensional, uncorrelated representations that maximally differentiate stimuli, and robust coding, which produces low-dimensional, smooth representations that generalize across stimuli. The decay of the eigenspectrum of the covariance matrix provides an intuitive perspective on this trade-off and has previously been observed to follow a critical power-law in the brain. While tuning curve heterogeneity has been proposed as a potential mechanism from which these power-laws could emerge, it remains unclear how specific biological properties of tuning curve heterogeneity give rise to them and how the organization of this heterogeneity maps onto the broader computational trade-offs between generalization, capacity, and noise robustness. In this work, we theoretically link tuning curve heterogeneity to spectral power-laws and use this biologically grounded model to investigate how different representations affect generalization, noise robustness, precision, and capacity in a linear decoder. We show mathematically that a population of Gaussian tuning curves with Gamma-distributed widths and a power-law relationship between peak firing rate and tuning width — both properties reflected in data from hippocampal place fields and V1 orientation tuning — is sufficient to produce power-law eigenspectra. This model can be used to construct tuning curve populations on the continuum between the robust and efficient coding schemes. These findings provide a biologically realistic explanation of spectral power-laws in neural populations, demonstrate the importance of tuning curve population statistics for neural coding, and allow for estimating the spectral decay from tuning curve statistics alone, circumventing the large populations and extensive stimulus sets typically required to directly compute this for noisy neural responses.

pending_articles.title: Neural correlates of executive functioning among adolescents and young adults living with HIV: a systematic review of structural and functional imaging studies
pending_articles.content: IntroductionReduced executive functioning (EF) - including inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, and working memory - has been frequently observed among adolescents and young adults living with HIV (AYALH), despite antiretroviral therapy (ART). These deficits may reflect HIV-associated alterations in brain structure and function. This review aimed to synthesize the available evidence of this relationship.MethodsFollowing the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, we searched PsycINFO, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases for relevant studies reporting EF outcomes and neural correlates (structural or functional).ResultsTwenty studies met the inclusion criteria. Significantly lower brain volumes and cortical thickness, lower fractional anisotropy, higher mean diffusivity, higher cerebral blood flow, and altered cerebral metabolites were observed among AYALH relative to matched controls. EF problems, particularly in working memory, were frequently reported. Overall, the observed neural alterations correlated with decreased EF among AYALH.ConclusionDespite ART use, HIV-associated neural alterations and executive function deficits still occur or persist among adolescents and young adults living with HIV. Preliminary evidence suggests that distinct HIV-associated neural alterations may be associated with EF problems in AYALH. Neuroimaging may offer insights into these cognitive difficulties, although more longitudinal and multimodal studies are needed.Systematic Review RegistrationThis review is registered in PROSPERO (https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/), registration number: CRD42025639283.

pending_articles.title: Cyborg dementia: could structural disembodiment accelerate brain aging via loss of muscle-bone trophic signaling? A matter of perspective
pending_articles.content: Advances in brain-machine interfaces and neuroprosthetics are often framed as a path toward overcoming the biological limits of the body, with the eventual replacement of failing limbs and organs by durable artificial substitutes. Interestingly, this optimistic narrative overlooks a challenge that is becoming increasingly apparent in aging neuroscience: brain health depends critically on a continuous supply of trophic signals originating from skeletal muscle and bone. Myokines and osteokines such as irisin, uncarboxylated osteocalcin, and cathepsin B act on the brain to sustain BDNF expression, synaptic plasticity, and neurogenesis, forming what has been described as a muscle-bone-brain axis; disuse and immobilization, even in the absence of any primary brain pathology, are sufficient to disrupt this signaling and accelerate cognitive decline. This raises a largely unaddressed question for cyborg technologies: could a robotic body, mechanically capable of movement but biologically inert and secreting none of the trophic factors that living muscle and bone normally provide, deprive the brain of signals it needs to remain healthy, thereby accelerating, rather than preventing, neural aging? We term this hypothetical condition cyborg dementia. Rather than a purely engineering problem of motor control and sensory feedback, this reframes brain-machine interface design as fundamentally about preserving the endocrine dialogue between brain and musculoskeletal system, extending the goals of neuroprosthetics beyond restoring action to protecting the neuroendocrine mechanisms that biological embodiment was silently providing all along.

recently_processed.title: An information theoretic approach to evaluating social behaviour in mice using automated home-cage monitoring
recently_processed.content: Background: Social behaviour in mice is commonly assessed using standardized assays such as the three-chambered task, which provide controlled measures of sociability but often capture behaviour over short timeframes that may not capture the complex behavioural repertoire exhibited in the home environment. Although automated home-cage monitoring enables continuous, longitudinal assessment of group-housed mice with minimal human interference, methods for quantifying social behaviour in this complex setting remain limited. Information theory offers a framework for measuring statistical dependence between animals but requires one to account for dependence related to the cage environment that arise even in the absence of social interaction. Methods: We developed an information-theoretic approach to quantify social dependence using longitudinal RFID-based positional data from group-housed mice monitored with automated home-cage monitoring system. Mutual information (MI) between cagemates was evaluated against a constrained null model that disrupted within-cage dependence while preserving individual movement patterns. We used two strains with known differences in sociability (C57BL/6J and BTBR) to assess sensitivity to various temporal sampling parameters, test-retest reliability, and correspondence with manually video-scored social behaviours. We further examined variation across genetic backgrounds and investigated relationships between home-cage measures, conventional behavioural assays (three-chamber sociability and open-field behaviour), and brain structure using in vivo MRI. Results: Observed MI was distinguishable from our null distribution, validating its use to quantify statistical dependence beyond that expected from shared cage constraints. MI recapitulated known differences in sociability between C57BL/6J and BTBR mice, showed high test-retest reliability, and correlated with independently video-scored social behaviours. Home-cage social measures also varied across genetic backgrounds and captured strain differences separate from three-chamber sociability. Furthermore, in vivo MRI revealed distinct neuroanatomical patterns for home cage compared to three-chamber sociability measures, including brain regions implicated in social behaviour. Comparisons with open-field measures further indicated that home-cage information-theoretic measures capture behavioural variation not fully represented by conventional measures of locomotion and exploration. Finally, social coordination exhibited distinct temporal dynamics across the circadian cycle. Conclusion: This study establishes and validates an information-theoretic framework for quantifying social dependence from longitudinal home-cage positional data. By accounting for dependence arising from shared environmental constraints and demonstrating reproducibility and correspondence with observed social behaviour, this approach provides a complementary method for characterizing social behaviour in mice. Its application across genetic backgrounds and temporal contexts offers opportunities to investigate behavioural variation beyond the restricted sampling of conventional assays.
